enhanced.fullText:
The OSHA Lead in Construction Standard, codified at 29 CFR § 1926.62, establishes comprehensive requirements for protecting workers from lead exposure during construction activities. This regulation applies with full force to higher education institutions conducting construction, alteration, repair, demolition, painting, or decorating activities on campus facilities.

Under 29 CFR § 1926.62(d), universities must conduct initial exposure assessments whenever employees may be exposed to lead concentrations at or above the action level of 30 micrograms per cubic meter (μg/m³) averaged over an 8-hour time-weighted average (TWA). The permissible exposure limit (PEL) is set at 50 μg/m³ as an 8-hour TWA, as specified in 29 CFR § 1926.62(c). When exposure monitoring indicates levels at or above the action level, universities must implement engineering controls, work practice controls, and respiratory protection programs.

The regulation's scope encompasses all construction work performed by university employees and contractors, including renovation of historic buildings, infrastructure projects, laboratory modifications, and maintenance activities involving lead-containing materials. Universities must establish written compliance programs under 29 CFR § 1926.62(e) when employee exposure exceeds the PEL, detailing specific methods and schedules for achieving compliance.

Medical surveillance requirements under 29 CFR § 1926.62(j) mandate that universities provide biological monitoring for employees exposed above the action level for more than 30 days per year. This includes blood lead level testing and zinc protoporphyrin measurements at specified intervals.

Training requirements under 29 CFR § 1926.62(l) require universities to provide comprehensive education programs covering health effects, exposure sources, protective measures, and regulatory requirements. Training must occur before initial assignment and annually thereafter.

Violations can result in OSHA citations with penalties up to $15,625 per serious violation and $156,259 for willful or repeat violations under 29 USC § 666. Universities must also comply with recordkeeping requirements under 29 CFR § 1926.62(n), maintaining exposure monitoring records for 30 years and medical surveillance records for the duration of employment plus 30 years. Recent updates have strengthened contractor oversight requirements and enhanced medical removal protection provisions.
enhanced.summary: OSHA's Lead in Construction Standard (29 CFR § 1926.62) requires universities to assess lead exposure during construction activities, implement controls when levels exceed 30 μg/m³, provide medical surveillance and training, and maintain comprehensive compliance programs.
enhanced.requirements:
## Exposure Assessment and Monitoring
- Conduct initial exposure assessments for all construction activities with potential lead exposure per 29 CFR § 1926.62(d)
- Perform periodic monitoring when exposure levels meet or exceed 30 μg/m³ action level
- Implement daily monitoring for exposures above permissible exposure limit of 50 μg/m³

## Engineering and Administrative Controls
- Establish written compliance programs when PEL is exceeded
- Implement engineering controls including HEPA filtration and containment systems
- Provide respiratory protection programs meeting 29 CFR § 1910.134 standards
- Designate regulated areas with appropriate signage and access controls

## Medical Surveillance and Training
- Provide medical examinations and biological monitoring for affected employees per 29 CFR § 1926.62(j)
- Conduct blood lead and zinc protoporphyrin testing at specified intervals
- Deliver comprehensive training programs before initial assignment and annually
- Implement medical removal protection for employees with elevated blood lead levels

## Contractor Oversight
- Ensure all contractors comply with lead standard requirements
- Verify contractor exposure assessments and control measures
- Coordinate multi-employer worksite safety responsibilities
enhanced.reportingRequirements: Universities must maintain exposure monitoring records for 30 years and medical surveillance records for employment duration plus 30 years per 29 CFR § 1926.62(n). Report work-related injuries and illnesses involving lead exposure to OSHA within required timeframes under 29 CFR § 1904.
